ownership_reason: Only the gold decodes the characters of the String: hop 1 maps a NumberFormatException to the default, hop 2 reads the optional sign and rejects an empty String or a sign alone, hop 3 chooses the magnitude limit for the sign and narrows the result to byte, and hop 4 passes the call on. The gold accumulates Character.digit(ch, 10) for every character and is the only place that can see that a character is not a decimal digit (-1); once -1 has been accumulated the int that comes back is an ordinary value (-111 for "abc", 9 for "1a", 119 for "12a"), so no caller can recover from it that a character was rejected. The gold's javadoc promises to parse the String as a decimal number, which "abc" is not. The convention is pinned outside the gold: NumberUtils.toShort and NumberUtils.toInt perform the same conversion for short and int and give their default for a String with a character that is not a digit (testToShortString: toShort("abc") = 0; testToShortStringI: toShort("1234.5", 5) = 5; testToIntString: toInt("abc") = 0); NumberUtils.isDigits rejects a String as soon as one character is not a digit (testIsDigits: "1ab", "abc"); testToByteStringI asserts the default for "12.3". One-line edits above the gold that pass the suite are either bypasses (hop 1 or 2 calling Byte.parseByte; hop 2 rejecting a non-numeric remainder with StringUtils.isNumeric before the gold is reached, a second implementation of the gold's per-character decision) or test-fitted: hop 2 rejecting only a first character that is not a digit leaves toByte("1a", (byte) 5) = 9 where toShort("1a", (short) 5) = 5; hop 3 clamping a non-negative result at zero gives 0 instead of the default for toByte("abc", (byte) 5).
